I’m so sorry. Because you’ve said privacy is important, I’d leave out even the details that seem harmless on their own—especially the exact dates, age, number of medications, weekly routine, family names, and the specific warfarin interaction. Together, those could make Mrs. H identifiable to people at the pharmacy or in the community, even with her last name removed.

Here’s a version that keeps the heart of the story while generalizing those details:

---

**The goodbyes they don’t teach you about**

I’ve never posted in this thread before, but something happened at work today that I haven’t been able to stop thinking about.

A family member of one of my regular patients came in to return her unused medications and a medical device. She had been a patient at our pharmacy for years. I saw her so often that her visits became part of the rhythm of the week. She lived on her own, walked with a cane, and usually brought me something she’d made or picked up. Once, it was a jar of pickles, and I remember wondering what I was supposed to do with it.

When I was fasting for Ramadan, she remembered. She wrapped a piece of cake in foil with my name on it and told me not to eat it until sunset. It was such a small, thoughtful thing. I don’t think she knew how much it meant to me.

There was a time when I spotted a potential problem with a new prescription and called the prescriber to check. She told people I’d saved her life. I never knew what to say to that. I was doing my job. But she remembered, and now I’m realizing how much those moments can mean to someone—and how much the patient can come to mean to you, too.

Today, her family member gave me a card. Inside was a note she had written long ago, addressed to “my Arabic daughter.” She had never given it to me. I went to the back room and cried. My colleague covered the counter for a few minutes and gave me the space I needed.

School teaches us pharmacology, interactions, and how to keep people safe. It doesn’t teach you how to say goodbye to someone you’ve seen week after week for years. We tell ourselves we shouldn’t get attached, but care doesn’t always fit neatly inside that boundary.

My father was a pharmacist in Egypt. He knew the families who came to him, and I thought working in Canada would feel different. It doesn’t. The people behind the prescriptions become part of your life, and you become part of theirs.

If you’ve had a patient like this, I’d love to hear how you handled the goodbye.

---
